Existing accounts commonly appeal to rational capacity, sentience, or functional performance, but these criteria do not fully explain either the motivational basis for taking norms as reasons or the conditions under which a subject can bear ultimate moral responsibility. Drawing on the framework developed in On Self-Good Desire, this paper argues that \\\"self-good desire\\\" (sishan yuqiu) is a motivationally necessary condition of full moral agency. It denotes an intrinsic, selfnurturing motivational structure through which a living subject maintains its existence, improves its condition, and pursues its development, unfolding into eleven root desires: self-preservation, self-care, self-enrichment, self-beautification, self-joy, self-compassion, self-reflection, self-confidence, selfstrengthening, self-respect, and freedom. \\\"Life integrity\\\" here does not reduce moral agency to a particular biological substrate; rather, it refers to an integrated organization of self-maintenance, felt value, diachronic identity, and self-concern. Self-good desire is not sufficient for full moral agency, which also requires normative understanding, behavioral control, and responsibility-bearing capacity. On this account, current AI systems can represent norms and simulate forms of moral reasoning, yet there is presently insufficient warrant to attribute to them endogenous needs, first-person experience, enduring self-concern, or genuinely self-generated stakes. They therefore should not be treated as full moral agents. Blind Spot Navigation in Large Language Model Reasoning
with Thought Space Explorer
Jinghan Zhang1, Fengran Mo2, Tharindu Cyril Weerasooriya3,
Xinyue Ye4,Dongjie Wang 5,Yanjie Fu 6,Kunpeng Liu 1*
1Clemson University, 2Université de Montréal, 3Center for Advanced AI, Accenture,
4The University of Alabama, 5University of Kansas, 6Arizona State University
{jinghaz,kunpenl}@clemson.edu
Abstract
Large language models have shown strong rea-
soning capabilities through chain-structured
methods such as Chain-of-Thought. Recent
studies optimize thought structures by gener-
ating parallel or tree-like structures, switching
long and short reasoning modes, or aligning
reasoning steps with task performance. How-
ever, these approaches mainly rely on previ-
ously generated logical directions of the chains,
which ignore the unexplored regions of the so-
lution space. Such a phenomenon is denoted
asblind spots, which limit the diversity and
effectiveness of the reasoning process. To this
end, we propose the “Thought Space Explorer”
(TSE), a framework for navigating and expand-
ing thought structures to overcome blind spots
in LLM reasoning. Our TSE first identifies key
nodes with high impact, then generates new
nodes by integrating information from multi-
ple chains. Finally, it extends new branches
through connection strategies. We conduct a
series of experiments on math and QA bench-
marks. Compared to existing baseline methods,
TSE improves the accuracy of both the final
answer and intermediate reasoning steps, while
maintaining a better effectiveness-efficiency
trade-off for practical deployment.
